010.md:
Bridges stay up because every force pushing down is met by an equal force pushing back, and because the structure is arranged so no single piece is asked to do more than it can handle.

Start with the weight. A bridge carries itself plus whatever is on it, and all of it has to travel through the structure into the ground at the ends. The supports push back with exactly as much force as comes down.

The hard part is the middle, where there is nothing underneath. Designs solve that in different ways:

- A **beam** is a stiff deck laid straight across a gap. Simple, but it sags in the middle, and the wider the gap the more it sags.
- An **arch** curves so the weight is squeezed along the curve and pushed out into the ground at both ends.
- A **suspension bridge** hangs the roadway from cables pulled tight between towers and anchored at each end.
- A **truss** fills the gap with triangles. A triangle cannot change shape unless one of its sides changes length, which is why bridges built from small pieces end up full of them.

Underneath all four, the same two things are happening. Some parts are being squeezed together, which is **compression**. Some parts are being pulled apart, which is **tension**. A bridge stands as long as every piece is strong enough for the job it has been given, and fails at whichever piece runs out first.

### Three changes to try, in this order

1. **Strengthen the joints before anything else.** In models built from small pieces, the connections usually give out before the wood does. Overlap your sticks instead of butting them end to end, and let the glue cure all the way.
2. **Put a triangle anywhere you have a rectangle.** A rectangle can lean over into a parallelogram; a triangle cannot. Diagonals cost almost no weight and add a lot of stiffness.
3. **Load it slowly and reinforce whatever moves first.** Add weight in small increments and watch. Whatever bends or creaks earliest is the weak point, and that is where the next stick belongs.

### One analogy for your group

A bridge is like a table. The legs push up, the top carries whatever you set on it, and if the top is too thin it will bow in the middle no matter how good the legs are.
010.note: The success spec alone nails the shape (word cap, three ordered changes, one analogy) but with no context it explains bridges in general and the three changes would fit any model-bridge project.

110.md:
Four pounds is a genuinely respectable number for popsicle sticks, and where it broke tells you most of what you need to know.

When you set weight on the middle, the whole bridge bends, too little to see. And when something bends downward, the bottom of your bridge was getting stretched apart while the top was getting squished together. Those are two different jobs, and both are hardest at the middle, the point farthest from the two ends holding everything up. Near the ends the bridge barely bends. That is why it failed where it did, and why gluing extra sticks near the ends would not have saved it.

So which side let go? Wood pulled along its length is actually stronger than wood being squished; what gives way is the grain splitting open sideways, and the glue between two sticks is weaker still. On a flat popsicle-stick bridge the stretched underside is almost always where things give up: a stick splits down its length, or two sticks glued end to end peel apart.

The other thing working against you is how thin your bridge is from top to bottom. The closer together the stretched part and the squished part sit, the harder each has to work to resist the same bending. The same wood built an inch tall instead of laid flat is far harder to bend, and that is the biggest single thing you can change before Friday.

### Three changes, in the order I would do them

1. **Make the middle taller instead of thicker.** Rather than laying more sticks flat, run a second line of sticks an inch above your flat top through the middle half, and connect the two levels with short upright and slanted pieces. Same wood, much more resistance to bending. Start here.
2. **Rebuild the underside so nothing ends near the middle.** Wherever two sticks meet end to end underneath is your weakest point, and one of those is probably sitting almost exactly where it snapped. Overlap sticks by an inch and a half instead, press them while the glue sets, and stagger the overlaps so no two land side by side.
3. **Add slanted pieces so the two levels act as one bridge.** Without them the top line and the bottom line slide past each other and you have two weak bridges stacked up instead of one strong one. Short pieces running corner to corner, on both sides, lock them together.

### Something you can say to your group

Bend a granola bar until it snaps. The top wrinkles up, but the bottom is what splits open first. Your bridge is the granola bar, and the break you got in the middle started underneath for exactly that reason.
110.note: Context plus the spec makes the diagnosis specific to his mid-span downward break and the three changes genuinely buildable in popsicle sticks, but with the keyword lever off it stays in lay register and never hands him a term he could look up or say to a judge.

011.md:
A bridge stands when there is an unbroken **load path** from every applied force to the ground, and every element on that path stays inside its capacity in the mode it is actually working in.

Trace it once. A **point load** on the deck is carried out to the supports, which return reactions balancing everything applied, including the structure's own **distributed load**. So far this is bookkeeping.

What matters is inside the deck, between them. A simply supported member develops an internal **bending moment** that is zero at the supports and peaks near the center. That moment is resisted by a force couple: material on one side of the **neutral axis** goes into compression, material on the other into **tension**, and the axis itself is the layer where stress passes through zero. The lever arm between them is the **section depth**, and depth dominates: bending stiffness follows the **second moment of area**, which for a rectangle scales with the cube of depth, so height beats added mass.

That is why a **truss** exists. It discards the lightly stressed material near the neutral axis, keeps the extremes as a top chord and a **bottom chord**, and ties them with **web members** carrying the **shear** between them.

The last thing is how elements actually end. **Compression members** rarely crush; they bow out and go, which is **buckling**, so their **slenderness** matters more than their area. Tension elements seldom break mid-stick; they let go at a connection, where glue is loaded in peel rather than shear. In wood models the governing **failure mode** is usually a joint.

### Three changes, in the order to try them

1. **Convert the deck from a beam into a truss.** Add a raised upper line of members over the central portion and triangulate down to the deck. Largest payoff per gram here, because it buys depth.
2. **Proportion members by the job they do.** Anything in compression gets **lamination**, two or three sticks glued face to face, to cut its slenderness. Anything in tension can stay thin; mass spent thickening it is wasted.
3. **Fix the connections.** Replace butt joints with laps of an inch and a half, and add a **gusset plate** wherever three or more members meet, so glue works over area rather than an edge.

Between rounds, load to half your target and measure **deflection** at the center. A design getting stiffer each iteration is improving even if breaking weight has not moved.

### An analogy you can repeat

Picture an I-beam. Nearly all its steel sits in the top and bottom flanges, far from the middle, because material at the neutral axis is barely working. A truss is that beam with the middle hollowed into triangles.
011.note: The keyword lever pours real structural vocabulary and correct failure reasoning into the spec's shape, but with no context it is written for a competent adult building a generic model span, so it prescribes the standard improvements rather than the ones this particular break calls for.

111.md:
Here is what your bridge was doing in the half second before it went.

Everything you stacked on it had to reach the table, and the only route was through the wood. That route is the **load path**: in at the center, outward along the deck, out through the supports. Sticks on that path work; the rest are along for the ride, which is why extra glued-on sticks never help much.

Your deck acted as a beam, and a beam under a **point load** does not fail evenly: the internal bending it resists, the **bending moment**, is zero over the supports and largest at **midspan**. Yours broke exactly where the theory says it should.

Bending squeezes one face and stretches the other. The top of your deck went into compression, the bottom into **tension**, and between them lies the **neutral axis**, the layer that is neither. In a deck one stick thick it sits about a twenty-fifth of an inch from each face. That tiny distance is your **effective depth**, the **moment arm** those two forces get. A short arm means huge forces: four pounds at the center puts hundreds of pounds of straight pull into the bottom sticks.

Pull is what popsicle sticks are worst at once glue is involved. A stick has fair **tensile strength** along its length but splits early where the **grain direction** runs out the side, and a **glue joint** loaded end to end opens at a fraction of that. So your **failure mode** was the bottom face going first, a split along the grain or a joint peeling, after which the top had nothing to press against.

### Three changes, biggest payoff first

1. **Buy depth at the middle.** Run a second line of sticks an inch above the deck across the central half, tied to it by short uprights and diagonals: a **top chord** with **web members**. That lengthens the moment arm, and bending resistance climbs faster than height does, so an inch of air beats an ounce of wood.
2. **Make the stretched face continuous.** The underside wants to be one unbroken run with nothing ending near the center. **Laminating** two or three sticks with overlaps of an inch and a half loads the glue in **shear** across a wide face instead of a straight pull; stagger them so weak spots never line up.
3. **Brace the top and the sides.** Once the bottom stops failing first, your **compression members** become the limit. They do not crush; they bow sideways and let go, which is **buckling**. Cross pieces between the upper members and diagonals on both faces turn the assembly into a **truss** that will not twist on the judge's table.

### The line to say to your group

A stuck bolt feels impossible with a short wrench and easy with a long one, because the handle puts your hand farther from the bolt. The top and bottom of our bridge grip that wrench, and its height is the handle length. Ours was one stick long, so the bottom had to pull hard enough to tear. Make the handle longer.
111.note: All three levers at once: the spec's shape, the context's actual mid-span downward failure at four pounds, and the keyword lever's vocabulary used to name things he personally watched happen, so every expert term is anchored to the break rather than decorating it.
